name: Emeka Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government, and we don't sell or campaign. Your words are confidential; public and private answers can differ. What does an ordinary workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and a senior developer at a tech company that writes software for water utilities. My team tracks faulty meter readings and makes sure an alert reaches the right repair crew. I review code, visit the control room sometimes, and mentor a new developer called Jonas. I have a master's degree, and I like seeing a screen decision turn into a fixed pipe rather than another report.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening outside work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife works in a bakery, and we have no children. I earn well for a developer, we have around eleven months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of software firms nearby. We help at a community repair day once a month. I use AI tools now and then, after I see somebody test them on an actual meter problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues to use the code helper for routine test cases and keep a person on every alert that sends a crew out. The water utility needs fewer false alarms, not a showpiece. A small saving in time would be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my work and my wife's bakery wage to continue. We have eleven months saved, so a slow release or unexpected bill wouldn't knock us over. I might even have more time to mentor Jonas if the routine checks get shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing the meter alerts with the control room and let the helper draft simple tests once we've checked its past results. We'd continue transferring money to savings after each pay day. In the first year I'd use the time saved for the monthly repair day and Jonas's training, not cut the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a tool that earns its place, and the household finances are steady. There is no reason to change our life around a little automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which false alarm sticks in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sensor once sent a crew to a dry street while a leaking pipe waited two streets away. I'd put that case in the helper's test set before trusting a new alert. The repair crew's time is not a spare resource.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does mentoring Jonas look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask Jonas to explain why a meter reading looks impossible before he changes the code. If the helper writes a test, he still has to show me the pipe record. That habit makes him useful to the utility.

say: I'd use **simple AI tests** only after checking past meter alerts with people.
I'd keep **human review** before software sends repair crews into the street.
think: I expect both **household wages** to continue and our eleven-month savings to absorb surprises.
I could spend more time **mentoring Jonas** if routine checks become shorter.
do: Keep **reviewing meter alerts** with the utility control room.
Continue **payday savings transfers** and use freed time for mentoring and community repair work.
feel: **Calm** about work and money with a modest, tested tool.
S0.quote: The repair crew's time is not a spare resource.
fieldNote: He judges AI by **false alerts**, linking screen work to a repair crew's wasted trip.
Higher pay and **eleven months saved** support his confidence under small change.
His interest in **mentoring Jonas** matches his view that practical learning matters.

steps.text: Keep reviewing meter alerts with the water utility control room
Continue household savings transfers after each pay day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we should test AI on customer messages and meter reports before changing staffing. I would ask the utility to measure wrong crew dispatches as well as speed. Jonas should still spend time with a repair crew. Software tests don't show a wet basement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company could need fewer developers once AI writes reports, code and replies. My senior role may shift to checking exceptions, but that could mean less paid work for me. My wife's bakery wage is real, yet it wouldn't replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd spend two paid afternoons learning the firm's new AI report tool on old meter incidents, with the utility supervisor checking the results. I'd ask my manager for a written staffing forecast and keep notes on errors. If developer hours fall during the first year, we'd cancel a planned holiday and I'd apply to nearby utility-software firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, although I can do something. Eleven months saved keeps a cut from becoming immediate trouble, but I still need a wage for the years after that. I don't want Jonas told his work is safe just because I can use the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the utility supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the tool's report with the day a crew went to the wrong street. If the report leaves out the delayed pipe repair, it's incomplete. I would ask the supervisor to mark the missing detail beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not switch to another local developer job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay while this team pays well and the trial gives us facts. If the hours are cut, I have other firms to ask. Leaving early would give up a good wage on a guess.

say: I'd demand **wrong-dispatch measures** before AI changes customer reports or staffing.
I'd keep **crew visits** in apprentice training so Jonas sees real water faults.
think: I could lose **paid hours** even if I become the person who checks exceptions.
My wife's **bakery wage** would not replace my higher developer income.
do: Learn the **new report tool** on past meter faults during two paid afternoons next month.
Request a **staffing forecast** and keep a record of omitted repair details.
Cancel the **planned holiday** and apply to nearby utility-software firms if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours, with savings and local openings offering control.
S1.quote: Software tests don't show a wet basement.
fieldNote: He agrees to use a **new AI tool** after old incidents and a utility supervisor provide a test.
He knows the **bakery wage** cannot carry their current household alone.
The holiday cancellation and local applications depend on **reduced hours**, not a forecast by itself.

steps.text: Learn the new AI report tool on past meter incidents during paid afternoons
Cancel the planned holiday if developer hours fall
Apply to nearby utility software firms if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company that full thinking AI by 2028 could write our code and answer the utility before robots reach physical repairs around 2031. I'd ask who will answer when a meter alert wrongly sends a crew. I wouldn't promise the team that our screens are protected by the pipes outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my higher developer wage could go. Eleven months saved and my wife's bakery job give us a bridge, but not a permanent replacement. The utility may still pay for someone to coordinate repair crews before robots arrive, yet I don't know how long that work lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the utility operations lead to let me shadow a repair dispatch shift during paid work time and request a reference from my manager. We'd pause our plan to buy a larger flat and keep the deposit available for living costs. In the first year after 2028, if my developer role ends, I'd apply for paid utility dispatch roles that actually exist; I'd take a short dispatch course only if required, affordable beyond eleven months of essentials, and offered before the robots of about 2031 narrow that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A year's savings sounds generous until the higher wage stops and every software firm has the same tool. I can look for a bridge, but I wouldn't pretend dispatch is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your wife about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife we should postpone the larger flat until we know what both wages look like. I'd show her the monthly rent on one bakery wage, then the amount our savings would have to cover. That is a family decision, not just my career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the community repair group for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether anyone knows of a paid opening at the utility, not ask the group to pay our rent. People there will tell me honestly what dispatch work involves. A favour is a lead, not a salary.

say: I'd ask who **owns wrong alerts** when 2028 thinking AI runs our utility code.
I'd explain that **2031 robots** follow later, while our screen work changes sooner.
think: I expect my **higher wage** could disappear across many software employers.
Our **eleven-month savings** and bakery income are a bridge, not permanent replacement pay.
do: Request **paid work time** to shadow utility dispatch and ask my manager for a reference this week.
Postpone the **larger flat** and keep its deposit available for essential bills.
Apply for **paid dispatch vacancies** after layoff; study only if required, affordable beyond eleven months, and timely before robots.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss despite savings and a possible temporary dispatch bridge.
S2.quote: A favour is a lead, not a salary.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 thinking AI** from robots reaching physical repair work around 2031.
The larger-flat plan changes because the **higher wage** may vanish; existing deposit money is not new saving.
A dispatch job and course require **real paid openings**, affordable training and a useful period before robots.

steps.text: Postpone buying a larger flat until both wages are clearer
Take a required affordable dispatch course before 2031 only if eleven months of essentials remain
Apply for paid utility dispatch vacancies if the developer role ends after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to publish a yearly plan for roles and to let developers spend time with utility crews. Five years gives us a chance to learn how dispatch decisions work before thinking AI reaches our screens in 2031. Robots around 2034 may then change the field work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into operations coordination if utilities still hire people for it, but I won't assume the job survives forever. I have a strong buffer and many local software firms; that lets me test a move while paid. My wife and I would not buy the larger flat on a promise of future income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next quarter I'd spend one paid day a month with the utility dispatch team and enroll in their certified operations course if my employer covers both the fee and paid work time. We'd keep the eleven-month emergency fund intact and put new savings into a separate housing account. In the first year after 2031, if my development hours shrink and a paid operations vacancy is open, I'd apply; if not, I'd keep my current wage and search locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives me room. I can learn from the crews without walking away from a good salary. The uncertainty is whether there will be a paid chair for me when the screens change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on the first dispatch day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow one low-pressure alert from the call to the crew's report and learn who decides whether a street needs digging. A code review doesn't teach me when a street needs digging. I'd write down where our current software makes the choice harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your employer refuses to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the paid dispatch days and ask which vacancies actually require the certificate. I wouldn't spend the emergency fund on a course just because it has a reassuring name. If a paid vacancy requires the certificate, I'd enroll using only new savings beyond eleven months of essentials.

say: I'd press for a **yearly role plan** and paid time with utility crews before 2031.
I'd remind coworkers that **2034 robots** may later change the field work too.
think: I could enter **operations coordination** if utilities still offer paid roles.
I won't buy a **larger flat** on the strength of a possible future wage.
do: Spend one **paid dispatch day** monthly next quarter and put new savings into a separate housing account.
Enroll in the **operations course** only with employer-paid fee and time, or when required vacancies and new savings protect eleven months.
Apply for **paid operations posts** if development hours shrink after 2031 and vacancies exist.
feel: **Anxious** about whether a paid operations seat will exist, despite time and savings.
S3.quote: A code review doesn't teach me when a street needs digging.
fieldNote: He values **crew judgment** learned on dispatch days, beyond what software testing teaches.
He keeps the **eleven-month fund** separate from possible housing money and course fees.
Operations training and applications remain tied to **funding and real vacancies**.

steps.text: Spend one paid workday monthly learning utility dispatch decisions
Take employer-funded paid-time course, or self-fund if vacancies require and eleven months’ essentials remain
Put new savings into a separate housing account while preserving emergency funds
Apply for paid operations vacancies if developer hours shrink after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas to learn why a water crew makes a call, not just how the alert screen works. A decade gives firms time to move people into new paid roles if they choose. Thinking AI in 2036 still reaches our code before physical robots appear around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could gain operations experience and save more by my late thirties. My wife's bakery job and our present buffer make today stable, though I wouldn't rely on either to replace my pay forever. I would judge a new role by its actual wages and working hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current developer job, the household savings transfer, and one paid utility visit a month if the firm agrees. I'd enroll in an operations certificate only if a paid vacancy requires it and the fee is covered by work or savings above eleven months of essentials. In the first year after 2036, if code roles contract, I'd apply for paid utility operations posts where they exist; otherwise I'd look among local employers before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The long stretch lets us plan without putting our life on hold today. I still feel a little sorry that skill in code might stop buying a secure wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the larger-flat plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We can save toward it, but we'd make an offer on a larger flat only after checking both current wages and the emergency fund. A better kitchen isn't worth losing room to breathe. My wife and I would make that choice together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave software before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer with work I understand. The best promise at the utility wouldn't cover our rent if the position didn't exist. I can learn steadily and still keep the wage I have.

say: I'd tell Jonas to learn **crew decisions**, not only alert-screen code.
I'd ask employers to use the **decade** to create paid transitions before 2036.
think: I could gain **operations experience** and savings while our present household remains secure.
I would judge any new role by **real pay and hours**, not a promise.
do: Keep the **developer wage** and savings transfer while taking paid utility visits if agreed.
Enroll in an **operations certificate** only if required by vacancies and funded without touching eleven months of essentials.
Apply for **paid utility posts** if coding roles contract after 2036; keep current work until an offer exists.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term coding wages, with present security and time to plan.
S4.quote: A better kitchen isn't worth losing room to breathe.
fieldNote: She would buy a larger flat only after checking **current wages and savings**, rather than a future job promise.
The operations certificate requires a **paid vacancy** and protected eleven-month buffer.
He would keep the developer wage until a **written paid offer** exists.

steps.text: Keep the paid developer job until a written alternative offer exists
Continue household savings transfers while current wages support them
Enroll in operations certificate only if paid vacancies require it and funding preserves eleven months' essentials
Apply for paid utility operations vacancies if coding roles contract after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our software work could disappear before I learn dispatch, and the bakery wage couldn't replace my pay. Written notice, paid time with utility crews and actual job openings would help us decide what to do without burning through savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the apprentice when an AI system writes every easy alert. My apprentice Jonas learned by watching a crew explain a false alarm, not by reading a perfect answer. I want that kind of paid learning kept open.

headlineQuote: My apprentice Jonas learned by watching a crew explain a false alarm, not by reading a perfect answer.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master's degree, leading water-utility software and mentoring a new developer.
He earns **higher pay**, shares eleven months of savings with his bakery-worker wife, and has many local software alternatives.
He uses AI **occasionally**, after real meter incidents show a tool works.
The **2028 shock** alarms him because his wage may end before a paid dispatch move is ready.
Longer timelines allow **funded operations training**, new housing savings and a search tied to real vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may end his coding wage before he learns dispatch and finds paid work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid utility-crew experience and actual job openings would protect the household's choices.
